summary: Presents a questionnaire about file systems on ARPANET hosts. A subcommittee led by Abhay Bhushan was drafting proposals for data transfer and file transfer protocols. They decided not to standardize file naming and access control for now, so users would need to know a remote system's conventions.

eli5.summary: Before making a rule for copying files, they ask each site how its file cabinet works, since every site names things differently.

questions: what was the file system questionnaire

subtitle: Survey of file system conventions across ARPANET sites.

tldr.problem: Early work on standardizing file transfer protocols revealed that ARPANET sites used completely different file naming, access control, and directory conventions. A standard protocol could not assume a universal file system model.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 180 is a questionnaire asking each ARPANET site to document their file system's naming conventions, access controls, directory structure, command functions, data representation, and I/O modes. The responses would inform protocol design decisions.
tldr.outcome: Rather than standardizing file naming across the network, the file transfer protocol would require users to know each remote site's local conventions, with NIC collecting and distributing documentation of those conventions.

today: RFC 180 represents a pivotal decision in early networking: instead of imposing a single file system model, the ARPANET chose to standardize the transfer mechanism and document the diversity of implementations. This approach enabled file sharing across heterogeneous systems and became a model for protocol design across the internet.

sections.title: The File Transfer Challenge
sections.content:
RFC 180 presents a questionnaire about file systems on ARPANET hosts. A subcommittee of the NWG, chaired by Abhay Bhushan, was drafting proposals for a data transfer protocol and a file transfer protocol. The subcommittee made a strategic decision: the file transfer protocol would support file transfer, but would not attempt to standardize file naming conventions, access control conventions, or other local file system practices.

This meant users would need to know and use each remote system's local file naming conventions and access procedures. To help users, comprehensive documentation of each site's file system was needed.
sections.eli5: Instead of making all computers use the same file names, they decided each site could keep its own system. But they wanted a big list of how each site's system worked.

sections.title: File System Information Requested
sections.content:
The questionnaire requested detailed information in six categories:

File naming conventions: The pathname syntax (the data string needed to identify a file), including typical components like device fields, user names, version numbers, index names, and punctuation. Default values like "device is disk" or "version number is the largest in system" were important to document.

Access control mechanisms: These ranged from simple knowledge of a pathname to elaborate hierarchies with passwords and separate read/write controls. Sites were asked to describe user inputs needed at file creation and retrieval, and the sharing implications (can two users update the same file simultaneously?).

Directories: Many systems maintained directories listing all files from a user or project, with file size and access control information. Sites were asked about directory syntax, contents, and access control.

Commands and functions: The RFC noted that some systems accepted whole files for sequential storage, while others allowed access to subfields with unique pathnames or provided restructuring and deletion functions.

Internal representation and I/O modes: Information about how data was encoded (ASCII, EBCDIC, or native word format) and whether alternate transmission modes would be useful (for example, a native mode for two PDP-10s that stored five characters plus one filler bit per word).
sections.eli5: They asked: How do you name a file? How do you control who can see it? Do you organize files in folders? What can you do with files? How is data stored inside?

sections.title: Documentation and Impact
sections.content:
Alex McKenzie of BBN was tasked with collecting responses from all ARPANET sites. Responses could include Xerox copies of short documentation sections if they were complete and comprehensible. The RFC included McKenzie's phone number for clarification: (617) 491-1850 ext. 441.

The collected information served dual purposes: it immediately provided network users with the knowledge needed to use remote file systems, and it informed the file transfer subcommittee's standards work by documenting the diversity of actual practice across the network. This pragmatic approach recognized that standardizing file system behavior was infeasible in the short term, but standardizing the transfer mechanism for diverse file systems was achievable.
sections.eli5: Each site sent back how their file system worked. Then the network could share that information so users knew what to expect, and it helped decide what the file transfer rules should be.

references.text: Postel, J., "Minutes of Network Working Group Meeting," RFC 164, 1971.
